Sales Objection Handling
How is our data protected, and how do you handle security?
We hold the data of more than 65 million consumers — more than a Telstra or an Optus. We go through penetration testing, we operate in the US which is very litigious, and we have a Master Service Agreement with Live Nation who've tried to break in and steal our data as part of their audit. AEG is the same — we passed all of their tests. We don't share your data with third-party advertisers or with other promoters. Your data is yours, and you can export it any time.
2h ago ·
|
Dismissed · Reason · just now by Jared
Sales Objection Handling
We need you to sign our contract and complete our vendor security questionnaire.
We've got 300 clients and we operate on one set of standard terms across all of them — even our largest clients at $500k to $1M sit on our existing terms. With a contract this size, getting our lawyer involved at $1,000 an hour just doesn't work. On the questionnaire, we'll do one for a $500k or $1M deal, but a War-and-Peace assessment on a $10k contract isn't viable. Happy to send our security one-pager and walk you through the enterprise audits we've passed — Live Nation, AEG, ICC Sydney, Venues NSW.
5h ago ·
|
Dismissed · Reason · just now by Jared
Sales Objection Handling
You're more expensive than what we're paying now.
It's worth thinking about what you're actually comparing. Tools like Mailchimp or ActiveCampaign are built for e-commerce — it's almost like buying a Honda Civic to drive an F1. They don't understand ticketing. The other thing is most of those platforms charge per send, which penalises you for using the platform. We're contact-based with unlimited sends. The real question is ROI — take that six grand and pump more tickets. We're confident we can increase ticket count and bring sales forward.
6h ago ·
|
Dismissed · Reason · just now by Jared
Sales Objection Handling
You don't integrate with our ticketing provider (e.g. Luma, Stripe, iTicket).
Two options. If we don't have a native integration with them yet, you can import a CSV file manually against the event — it's not too challenging, you drag the CSV into orders and as long as there's an email address attached, we match and bind all the data. The other path is API. We've now opened up our API integration — a small US ticketing company built one in about three weeks. We're also integrated natively with Ticketmaster, Tixr, Moshtix, OzTix, Humanitix, Eventbrite, Try Booking, Ticketek and Universe.
9h ago ·
|
Dismissed · Reason · just now by Jared
Sales Objection Handling
Can you do [specific feature X]?
Honest answer — I don't believe that exists yet. I actually haven't been asked that question before, so let me check whether it's on the roadmap. In the meantime, here's a workaround that gets you most of the way there: [tags / CSV import / custom field / manual sync, depending on which feature]. For refund data on Universe specifically, that's not something we can pull through their API — it's a limitation on their side, not ours.

Dismissed · Reason · just now by Jared
Sales Objection Handling
We need indemnity in the contract.
It's an easy one — we don't provide any indemnity. Audience Republic is indemnified, but we don't provide indemnity to our clients. I know it's not the answer your legal team wants to hear, but it's our standard terms and it's the same position we hold with every client we work with, including our enterprise tier at $500k to $1M.
1d ago ·

Dismissed · Reason · just now by Jared
Updated Sales Objection Handling
Can you match the price we're paying our current provider?
We don't price-match — and it's worth being upfront about why. Most of those platforms charge per send, so the number you're quoting isn't really comparable to a contact-based plan with unlimited sends. What we can do is structure the ramp: a 12-month term at your current contact volume, with that rate locked for year two. For multi-year deals above $50k we can also bring forward onboarding credits. The real lever is ROI — if we increase ticket count, the price difference disappears.

Resolved Renewal Risk Signals
Accounts receiving regular structured engagement renew significantly more often than those without — quarterly business reviews drive a 22% lift, monthly check-ins drive 19%. Consistent engagement matters more than the specific cadence; either rhythm prevents the gap during which problems can harden into churn decisions.

Merged from 2 competing patterns · resolved just now by Jared ·

just now ·
Dismissed · Reason · just now by Jared
You're all caught up
Resolve conflict
Statement A
Accounts that receive quarterly business reviews renew 22% more often than those without.
The effect holds across the mid-market segment and strengthens with deal size. Every account lost in the last year had either skipped its QBR or rescheduled it more than twice — the review reliably surfaces renewal risk early enough for the CSM to intervene. No additional lift was seen for cadences shorter than quarterly.
2w ago ·
vs
Statement B
Accounts with monthly check-ins renew 19% more often than those without.
The shorter interval keeps the CSM close enough to catch problems before they compound. The lift is most pronounced for newer accounts in their first renewal cycle, where a quarterly gap is long enough for an unaddressed issue to harden into a churn decision.
3w ago ·

Raw data access

Whether destinations can reach the underlying raw data, in addition to verified intelligence.

Off by default

When on, destinations like the Assistant can search the underlying transcripts, messages, and emails — not just verified intelligence. Verified intelligence always takes precedence; raw data is only consulted when no pattern fits.

Trade-off: better answers in long-tail cases, but slower responses and a higher chance of returning unverified content. Most teams leave this off and verify more patterns instead. Destinations using this View can also choose to opt-out per session.

Danger zone

Destructive actions — some can't be undone.

When to use a briefing vs a workflow
Briefings deliver scheduled or event-triggered summaries drawn from this View — they roll up patterns into a digest. Workflows take individual actions when a trigger fires (post to Slack, create a Jira ticket, update Salesforce). If you're sending the same recurring summary to a person or channel, use a briefing.

Labels vs. folders

A View can have many labels. Labels work across Views — folders don't. Use them for cross-cutting themes like teams, campaigns, or quarters.

Dev note
Keep Labels parallel-ready to Views. We're shipping Labels as lightweight metadata for now — settings only, no surface area beyond this page. There's a real chance we'll later extend the View pattern to Labels (a Label hub with its own filtered feed, the ability to point Destinations like Briefings or the Assistant at a Label, possibly even an "auto-apply rules" surface). Build so that's additive, not a rewrite:
  • Store owner, visibility, and access on Labels with the same shape as Views.
  • Treat label_id as a first-class scope token anywhere we currently accept view_id (Assistant scope, saved feeds, Destinations, Workflows).
  • Avoid hardcoding "label = filter chip" in APIs or routes — give Labels their own resource path so a future /labels/:id/feed or /labels/:id/destinations doesn't require schema migration.
  • Permission checks for "can apply this label" should read from the Label's access record, not be derived from View access.

Can you match the price we're paying our current provider?
We don't price-match — and it's worth being upfront about why. Most of those platforms charge per send, so the number you're quoting isn't really comparable to a contact-based plan with unlimited sends. What we can do is structure the ramp: a 12-month term at your current contact volume, with that rate locked for year two. For multi-year deals above $50k we can also bring forward onboarding credits. The real lever is ROI — if we increase ticket count, the price difference disappears.

Dev note
Read state is per-user. Verification state is team-wide. The Unread divider, the read/unread flag on a card, and "Mark all read" are all personal — each user has their own read cursor against the same shared statements. Confirm / Disagree / Refine, by contrast, mutate the statement itself and apply for everyone with access to the View. Implementation guidance:
  • Store read state on a join table — user_id × statement_id × seen_at — not as a flag on the statement.
  • Unread counts on the divider, in the sidebar, and in any digest must be computed per the requesting user.
  • Verification actions write to the statement's lifecycle (candidate / promoted / contested / verified / deprecated) and are visible to all members instantly.
  • If a teammate has already confirmed/disagreed/refined a statement that's still in your unread queue, the card should surface that on its meta line (e.g. ✓ Confirmed by Sarah · 2h ago) so you don't double-handle it. The action is still available, but the team has it covered.
  • Treat read state as best-effort: viewing the feed marks visible cards as read after a short dwell; opening the detail view marks immediately. Don't gate workflows on it.

Notes on the email system
Cadence vs trigger · Two scheduled (Briefing daily, Digest weekly), three event-triggered (Conflict, Promotion, Mention). The user can switch Briefing to weekly or off; Digest can be monthly. Event emails are throttled — never more than one Conflict alert per View per day.
Same voice as the app · "Confirmed by", "Now powering", "canonical" — emails reuse the in-app vocabulary so the relationship between the email and the feed is obvious. No marketing-speak.
Personal vs team · Briefing and Mention are personal ("your queue", "you were mentioned"). Digest is shared (team-wide stats). Promotion is team-news with personal framing.
Action over inbox-zero · Each email has one primary CTA that takes you to the right surface in the app. No "view all", no "see more" stuffing — the email is a delivery surface, not a destination.
Safe to skim · The first ~80 chars (subject + preview) tell you what's inside. If you only read those, you still know if you need to open Neuma.
Mute granularity · Every email footer offers a mute that matches the email's scope — mute this View's promotions, mute this thread, switch to weekly. Notifications never feel like all-or-nothing.

Handling the “too expensive” objection

DO MR JK
Maintained by the Sales team · kept current by Neuma
Auto-updating destination
Fed by the Sales Objection Handling View

This page is a destination — intelligence is sent here, it isn't written here. The sections marked Live below are assembled from verified statements in the source View, and they re-write themselves whenever that intelligence changes. The team adds editorial context around them; Neuma keeps the facts current.

12 verified statements feeding this page 3 live sections · 2 editorial Open source View

Price is the most common objection in mid-market deals, and the one reps most often get wrong by negotiating against it directly. This page collects what's actually working — drawn from recorded calls, not theory. Sections tagged Live are kept current by Neuma; the editorial sections are the team's interpretation of them.

What prospects actually mean Live
From verified intelligence 2 statements
When a prospect says “too expensive,” 7 in 10 are benchmarking against Northstar's Starter tier — a plan with roughly half our feature set, not an equivalent one.
A price objection raised before a live demo is roughly 3× less likely to reach a close than the same objection raised after one.
Synced from 23 calls · 6 reps · confirmed by 4 teammates
The reframe that works Live
This section updated 4 minutes ago — confidence rose to High after 3 new calls this week confirmed the pattern. See what changed →
Updated · from verified intelligence 1 statement
Reframing the conversation around annual value delivered rather than monthly cost resolves the objection in about 60% of recorded calls.
Synced from 31 calls · last change 4m ago
A recommended opening Editorial
“I hear you — let's make sure that number maps to the outcome. Most teams your size see payback inside the first quarter. Before we talk price, can we walk through what that quarter is worth to you?”
DO Written by Dana Olsen · edited 6 days ago
When to hold firm Editorial

If a prospect anchors on price before seeing the product, that's a discovery gap, not a pricing problem — route them back to a demo rather than discounting. Discounting this early trains the buyer to expect more, and the live data above shows the objection usually dissolves once value is established.

Live sections re-check whenever their source intelligence changes — not on a timer. “Synced 4m ago” means nothing has changed in the last 4 minutes. Editorial sections change only when a teammate edits them.
Notes on the wiki destination
A destination, not a doc · The page is wired to a View. Verified intelligence flows in and the live sections stay current with zero manual upkeep — the wiki is where intelligence is read, the feed is where it's made.
Live vs editorial, per section · Every section is one or the other. Live sections are owned by Neuma; editorial sections by people. A page mixes both, but a single section never has two owners — that's what makes auto-update safe.
No silent drift · When a live section changes, the page surfaces what changed and when. Readers trust the page because they can see it's fresh, instead of wondering whether it's stale.
Sync is event-driven · Live sections re-check when their source intelligence is re-verified, not on a clock. The “Synced 4m ago” pill reuses the same status component as the feed and statement pages.
Edit conflicts can't happen · Because each section has exactly one owner, Neuma never overwrites a person's words. Editing a live section opens a suggestion against the source View rather than a local override.
Provenance travels with content · Each live section keeps its source count, contributors and verification state visible — so the wiki carries the same trust signals a reader would see in the feed.

What v2 changes
Names the contradiction · An agree / differ pair states the conflict in one read — both statements predict renewal; they only clash on cadence. The reader never has to infer the tension.
Previews every outcome · Each option reveals exactly what the feed card will say once applied — not just Merge. No resolution is a leap of faith.
Shows the blast radius · The statement is live in 3 Views; v2 names them before you commit, so a cross-View change is never a surprise.
Surfaces human validation · Each statement shows who confirmed it — a conflict between two trusted reads is a judgement call, and you should see whose judgement is already behind each side.
Offers an exit from deciding alone · "Discuss with team" is a first-class action — not every conflict should be resolved by whoever opened the modal.
Still closes the loop · Apply confirms inline and the feed card flips to its resolved state with an Undo — carried over from v1.
